1.pericope_label: The law of the Nazarite introduced: a man or woman separating themselves unto the Lord

schools.summary: Gill says the Lord spake unto Moses at the same time, or immediately after the law concerning the woman suspected of adultery was given, with which the following law concerning Nazarites may be thought to have a close connection, as some Jewish writers observe, women being concerned in it as well as men; and as wine leads to adultery, as Jarchi observes, abstinence from it, which the Nazarite's vow obliged to, and forbearance of trimming and dressing the hair, and a being more strictly and closely devoted to the service of God, were very likely means of preserving from unchastity, and any suspicion of it. The following law concerned only the children of Israel and not Gentiles, Gill says, so runs the Jewish canon: the Gentiles have no Nazariteship, and though they may bring their vows and freewill offerings as an Israelite, yet if they vow the vow of a Nazarite the law of the Nazarite is not obliging on them, nor are they bound by it, but it is free for them to drink wine and to defile themselves for the dead, for it is written, speak unto the children of Israel. Calvin says that God recently appointed a tribute for every soul, whereby the Israelites were to acknowledge that they were his children, and that by that profession he bound them all to himself from the least to the greatest; a closer tie of obligation is now treated of, when any should voluntarily devote himself to God for a season. These were called Nazarites, Calvin says, because there was greater dignity or excellence in them than in the common people, for they were as ornaments to the Church, and God willed that his peculiar glory should shine brightly in them. When Amos expostulates with them because they had prevented the prophets from exercising their office and had corrupted the Nazarites with wine, he says, in amplification of their crime, that they had been honoured with a special blessing when God had created of their sons Nazarites and prophets; and when Jeremiah deplores the desolation of the Church he insists on this corruption, that their Nazarites no longer appeared as of old, purer than snow. Nor is it to be doubted, Calvin says, that when Jacob distinguished Joseph his son by the title of a Nazarite among his brethren he alluded in the spirit of prophecy to that degree of honour in which afterwards, under the Law, they stood who separated themselves unto God, as the lights of the Church. Therefore, although this consecration pertained not to the whole people, it should be deservedly reckoned amongst the exercises of piety, because the Nazarites were like standard-bearers to show others the way; and though they did not attract all to follow their example, yet the ardour of their zeal was of no little advantage to the weak and inexperienced, exciting them forwards according to their capacity. Now, because God abominates all fictitious worship, Calvin says, he put a restraint on their licentiousness by giving them a clear and certain rule; and from the testimony of Amos it is gathered that God alone was the appointer of the Nazarite vow. We must remember, then, that the Nazarites shone among the people of God like precious jewels, and although few imitated them, yet they were as standard-bearers and leaders to awaken zeal amongst the multitude for the service of God. We must observe, by the way, Calvin adds, that Samson was a Nazarite of another kind, because he did not take the vow upon him only for a season but was sanctified from the womb for his whole life, and separated from the rest of the people, in which respect too he was a type of Christ and represented him. And surely whatever is here taught should be referred to the sole Fountain of sanctity, as if the image of Christ had been set before the eyes of the Jews in a mirror; for the nearer anyone under the Law approached to God, the more did Christ shine forth in him. We know that the whole priesthood of the Law was nothing but his image, Calvin says, and the same may be said of the Nazarites, whose purity and abstinence ornamented them with peculiar dignity.

Matthew Henry says that after the law for the discovery and shame of those that by sin had made themselves vile, fitly follows this for the direction and encouragement of those who by their eminent piety and devotion had made themselves honourable, and distinguished themselves from their neighbours. It is very probable, Henry says, that there were those before the making of this law who went under the character of Nazarites, and were celebrated by that title as persons professing greater strictness and zeal in religion than other people, for the vow of a Nazarite is spoken of here as a thing already well known, but the obligation of it is reduced to a greater certainty than hitherto it had been; and Joseph is called a Nazarite among his brethren not only because separate from them but because eminent among them. The general character of a Nazarite is that he is a person separated unto the Lord, Henry says: some were Nazarites for life, either by divine designation, as Samson and John the Baptist, or by their parents' vow, as Samuel, and of these this law speaks not; others were so for a certain time and by their own voluntary engagement, and concerning them rules are given by this law. A woman might bind herself with the vow of a Nazarite, under the limitations found in the thirtieth chapter. The Nazarites were devoted to the Lord during the time of their Nazariteship, Henry says, and it is probable spent much of their time in the study of the law, in acts of devotion, and instructing others, so that an air of piety was put upon them and upon their whole conversation; they were separated from common persons and common things, for those that are consecrated to God must not be conformed to this world, and they distinguished themselves not only from others but from what they themselves were before and after; and they separated themselves by vowing a vow, for every Israelite was bound by the divine law to love God with all his heart, but the Nazarites by their own act and deed bound themselves to some religious observances, as fruits and expressions of that love, which other Israelites were not bound to. Some such there were, Henry says, whose spirits God stirred up to be in their day the ornaments of the church, the standard-bearers of religion, and patterns of piety; it is spoken of as a great favour to their nation that God raised up of their young men for Nazarites, and the Nazarites were known in the streets and respected as purer than snow, whiter than milk. Christ was called in reproach a Nazarene, and so were his followers, Henry says, but he was no Nazarite according to this law, for he drank wine and touched dead bodies; yet in him this type had its accomplishment, for in him all purity and perfection met, and every true Christian is a spiritual Nazarite, separated by vow unto the Lord. We find St Paul, by the persuasion of his friends and in complaisance to the Jews, submitting to this law of the Nazarites, Henry notes, but at the same time it is declared that the Gentiles should observe no such thing. It was looked upon as a great honour to a man to be a Nazarite, he adds, and therefore if a man speak of it as a punishment, saying for instance that he will be a Nazarite rather than do so or so, he is, say the Jews, a wicked man; but he that vows unto the Lord in the way of holiness to be a Nazarite, lo, the crown of his God is upon his head. That the fancies of superstitious men might not multiply their restraints endlessly, Henry says, God himself lays down the law for them and gives them the rule of their profession. There is nothing in Scripture, Henry writes, that bears the least resemblance to the religious orders of the church of Rome except these Nazarites; but mark the difference, or rather how completely opposed. The religious of that church are forbidden to marry, but no such restriction is laid upon the Nazarites; they are commanded to abstain from meats, but the Nazarites might eat any food allowed other Israelites; they are not generally forbidden wine, not even on their fasting days, but the Nazarites might not have wine at any time; their vow is lasting, even to the end of their lives, but the Nazarites' vow was only for a limited time, at their own will, and in certain cases not unless allowed by husbands or parents. Such a thorough difference there is, Henry concludes, between rules of man's invention and those directed in Scripture; and let us not forget that the Lord Jesus is not only our Surety but also our example, for whose sake we must renounce worldly pleasures, abstain from fleshly lusts, be separate from sinners, make open profession of our faith, moderate natural affections, be spiritually-minded and devoted to God's service, and desirous to be an example all around us.

Keil and Delitzsch say that the words with which the law is introduced, if a man or woman make a separate vow, a Nazarite vow, to live consecrated to the Lord, show not only that the vow of the Nazarite was a matter of free choice, but that it was a mode of practising godliness and piety already customary among the people. The word for Nazarite, from a root meaning to separate, means literally the separated, and is applied to the man who vowed that he would make a separation to Jehovah, that is, lead a separate life for the Lord and his service. The origin of this custom is involved in obscurity, Keil says: there is no certain clue to indicate that it was derived from Egypt, for the so-called hair-offering vows are met with among several ancient tribes, for which he refers to Spencer and to Knobel, and have no special relationship to the Nazarite, whilst vows of abstinence were common to all the religions of antiquity. The Nazarite vow was taken at first for a particular time, at the close of which the separation terminated with release from the vow, and this is the only form contemplated here. The vow consisted of three points, Keil says, of which the first was that he was to abstain from wine and intoxicating drink, and neither to drink vinegar of wine or of strong drink, nor any juice of the grape, which is literally the dissolving of grapes, that is, fresh must pressed out, nor to eat fresh grapes or dried; in fact, during the whole period of his vow he was not to eat of anything prepared from the vine, from the kernels even to the husk, that is, not the smallest quantity of the fruit of the vine. Ellicott says the clause is better rendered, when a man or woman shall make a special or singular vow, the vow of a Nazirite, as in Leviticus; the verb which is used denotes the doing of something wonderful or extraordinary, and the spiritual lesson seems to be that Christ's servants are expected and required to do something more than others. The vows here referred to were made for a specific period, Ellicott says, though at a later time some were consecrated or set apart as Nazirites during the entire period of their lives, as in the case of Samson, Samuel and John the Baptist, this consecration appearing to have been made rather as the result of Divine revelation than of arbitrary appointment on the part of their parents; and the meaning of the word Nazirite is contained in the concluding words of the verse, to separate himself unto Jehovah, where the cognate verb is used.

Adam Clarke sets out the argument of the chapter, that it gives the vow of the Nazarite and what it consisted in, how he is to be purified when accidentally defiled, the sacrifices he is to bring and the rites he is to perform when the vow of his separation is fulfilled, the manner in which the priests are to bless the people, and the putting of the name of the Lord on the children of Israel, whom he promises to bless. The Hebrew word, from a root meaning to separate, signifies merely a separated person, Clarke says, that is, one peculiarly devoted to the service of God by being separated from all servile employments. From the Nazarites sprang the Rechabites, Clarke says, from the Rechabites the Essenes, from the Essenes the Anchorites or Hermits, and in imitation of those, the different monastic orders. Some contend strongly that the Nazarite was a type of our Lord, he continues, but neither analogy nor proof can be produced: our blessed Lord both drank wine and touched the dead, which no Nazarite would do, and as to his either shaving his hair or letting it grow we know nothing. His being called a Nazarene in Matthew is nothing to the purpose, Clarke says, as it can mean no more than either that he was an inhabitant of Nazareth, which was a place of no credit and therefore used as a term of reproach, or that he was in a general sense consecrated to the service of God, as were Samson, Samuel, Jeremiah and John the Baptist; or rather that he was the netser or Branch of Isaiah and the tsemach of Zechariah, which is quite a different word, and this title is expressly applied to our blessed Lord by those prophets, but in no place do they or any other prophets call him a Nazarite in the sense in which the Hebrew nazir is used. Indeed it could not in truth be applied to him, Clarke says, as the distinguishing marks of a Nazarite never belonged to him; he was, it is true, the branch out of the root of Jesse, the genuine heir to the throne of David, whose dominion should extend over the universe, who should be King of kings and Lord of lords, but the Greek word in Matthew signifies merely a Nazoraean, or inhabitant of Nazareth. Wesley says that both sexes might make this vow if they were free and at their own disposal, since otherwise their parents or husbands could disannul the vow; and that by the vow of a Nazarite they sequestered themselves from worldly employments and enjoyments, that they might entirely consecrate themselves to God's service, and this either for their whole lifetime or for a less and limited space of time.

debates: Whether the Nazarite typified Christ: Calvin says Samson, sanctified from the womb, was a type of Christ and represented him, and that the nearer anyone under the Law approached to God the more did Christ shine forth in him; Clarke denies it outright, since our Lord drank wine and touched the dead, and separates the prophets' word for branch, which is applied to him, from the word for a separated person, which is not; Henry takes a middle place, that Christ was no Nazarite according to this law yet in him the type had its accomplishment

Whether the vow was customary before the law: Keil holds that the wording shows it already customary among the people, though its origin is involved in obscurity and no certain clue points to Egypt; Henry agrees that it is spoken of as a thing already well known, the law only reducing its obligation to a greater certainty; Calvin argues from Amos that God alone was the appointer of the vow, and that he gave a clear rule precisely because he abominates all fictitious worship

What the Nazarite institution became afterwards: Clarke traces a descent from the Nazarites through the Rechabites and the Essenes to the Anchorites and the monastic orders; Henry allows this the only resemblance in Scripture to the religious orders of Rome and then opposes it on four counts, marriage, meats, wine and the duration of the vow

Why the law follows the law of jealousy: Gill reports the Jewish view that the connection is close, since women are concerned in both and, wine leading to adultery, the Nazarite's abstinence guarded against suspicion of unchastity; Henry makes the sequence a deliberate contrast between those who by sin had made themselves vile and those who by piety had made themselves honourable
outliers: Calvin's figure of the Nazarites as precious jewels and standard-bearers, whose zeal advantaged the weak and inexperienced even where it was not imitated
Gill's citation of the Jewish canon that the Gentiles have no Nazariteship, remaining free to drink wine and to defile themselves for the dead
Henry's four-count comparison of the Nazarite vow with the religious orders of Rome, on marriage, meats, wine and duration
Henry's report of the rabbinic saying that he who calls the vow a punishment is a wicked man, but he that vows in the way of holiness has the crown of his God upon his head
Keil's appeal to Spencer and Knobel that hair-offering vows are found among several ancient tribes, so that no Egyptian derivation can be established

The conjecture of the learned Dr Lightfoot, repeated by Henry, that the order represented man's state in innocency and that the forbidden tree was the vine, so that those who gave Nazarites wine did the tempter's work

3.pericope_label: The three abstentions: wine and every product of the vine, and the razor forbidden

schools.summary: Gill says the Nazarite was to separate himself from wine, old or new, as Ben Gersom says, from drinking any of it: not only from an immoderate and excessive drinking of it, which every man should abstain from, but from drinking of it at all, that he might be more free and fit for the service of God, for prayer, meditation, reading the Scriptures and attendance on the worship of God in all its branches, and be less liable to temptations to sin; for, as Aben Ezra observes, many transgressions are occasioned by wine, which, if drunk immoderately, intoxicates the mind and unfits for religious duties, excites lust, and leads on to many vices. All the days of his separation he was to eat nothing that is made of the vine tree, Gill says, of its leaves, branches and fruit, especially the last, put into any sort of food, or infused into any liquor, or mixed with any sauce for food; the days or time of separation were according as the vow was made, for a shorter or longer time, though the Jews say that where the vow is absolutely expressed it is always to be understood of thirty days, during which time the Nazarite was not to eat or drink of any composition that had anything of the vine in it. Be the time he has vowed to be a Nazarite a week, a month, or more, even a thousand days, Gill adds, it was not to be less than thirty, as Ben Gersom observes. Calvin says the first injunction is that they should not only abstain from wine but should not even taste grapes or anything connected with wine. The simple observance was that they should not drink wine or anything inebriating, Calvin says, but because men are crafty in inventing subterfuges it was necessary to express specifically the means whereby the Law might be defrauded; thus, in abstaining from wine, they would not have deprived themselves of luxuries, either by indulging in fresh or dried grapes, or by mixing water with grapes and expressing their juice, or by imitating the sweetness of wine by other delicate preparations. Hence it appears how many secret recesses and lurking-places are possessed by man's hypocrisy, Calvin says, whilst it shamelessly imagines stupid means of deception for cheating God himself; but at the same time we must remark that this subtlety was intolerable to God, who is pleased by nothing so much as sincerity. We shall also see elsewhere that the priests, when they were executing their office by turns in the Temple, were forbidden the use of wine, Calvin says, and this similarity proves what he has already said, that the Nazarites were thus separated from the multitude that they might approach to the honour of the priesthood. But abstinence from wine was enjoined not only that they might avoid drunkenness, but that their whole mode of living might be more temperate and frugal, Calvin says, for the drinking of wine is well known to be among the chief pleasures of the table, and those who are not abstentious will rather content themselves with moderate and common food than bear to be deprived of wine. We may then learn from hence that a sober use of wine is a most important part of temperate living, and that in all gluttony and intemperance this is most to be condemned, when men have too great a love of excess in wine-drinking. It is then astonishing, Calvin says, that when the monks under the Papacy boast of their angelical perfection, they should with one accord refuse to abstain from wine; with the Carthusian monks it is sinful to touch during their whole life a bit of beef or pork, and they would glory in being martyrs if they obstinately preferred to die rather than to eat meat in a case of necessity, but their temperance is so inconsistent that this austerity as to food acquires for them the greater licence in drinking, as if they purposely avenged themselves in this way. Wherefore nothing can be more insufferable than their boasting, Calvin concludes, since this abstinence in eating alone is a mere mockery of God.

Charles Ellicott says the law of the Nazirite in this respect, as in regard to defilement from the dead, was more strict than that which was enjoined upon the priests, thus typifying the entire surrender of the heart and life to God, and freedom from the distraction of earthly ties. The ideal of this separation, however, Ellicott says, was not that of a life of monastic seclusion, but of action, and of uninterrupted devotion to the Divine service; the priests were forbidden to drink wine or strong drink when they entered the tabernacle to perform service there, but were not prohibited the use of wine at other times. Strong drink is supposed to have been made of barley and dates or honey, he says; and the prohibition to eat any of the produce of the vine, even of that which was not intoxicating, seems designed to denote the entire consecration of the Nazirite to the Divine service, and the obligation which rested upon him to abstain from all the desires and delights of the flesh, the love of cakes made of raisins being coupled in Hosea with idolatry. Of the words closing the prohibition Ellicott says the first, rendered kernels, is supposed by some to denote sour grapes and by others the kernels of berries, while the second denotes the shell or husk. Keil and Delitzsch say that, secondly, during the whole term of his vow of consecration no razor was to come upon his head: till the days were fulfilled which he had consecrated to the Lord he was to be holy, and to make great the free growth of the hair of his head. The free growth of the hair is called the diadem of his God upon his head, Keil says, like the golden diadem upon the turban of the high priest and the anointing oil upon the high priest's head; by this he sanctified his head to the Lord, so that the consecration of the Nazarite culminated in his uncut hair.

Adam Clarke says the Hebrew word rendered vinegar signifies fermented wine, and is probably used here to signify wine of a strong body, or any highly intoxicating liquor. He reports the supposition of a learned writer that, the leper being the most defiled and loathsome of creatures and an emblem of the wretched state of man by the fall, the Nazarite was the emblem of man in his state of innocence, and that wine and grapes are here particularly forbidden to the Nazarite because, being an emblem of man in his paradisiacal state, he was forbidden that tree and its fruits by eating of which Adam fell, the writer, as well as the Jewish rabbins, believing the tree of knowledge to have been none other than the vine. Clarke sets out the vow in six particulars: that the man consecrated himself in a very especial and extraordinary manner to God; that this was to continue for a certain season, probably never less than a whole year, that he might have a full growth of hair to burn in the fire which is under the sacrifice of the peace-offering; that during the time of his separation he drank no wine nor strong drink, nor used any vinegar formed from any inebriating liquor, nor ate the flesh or dried grapes, nor tasted even the kernels or husks of anything that had grown upon the vine; that he never shaved his head but let his hair grow, as the proof of his being in this separated state and under vows of peculiar austerity; that he never touched any dead body nor did any of the last offices, even to his nearest kin, but was considered as the priests, who were wholly taken up with the service of God and regarded nothing else; and that all the days of his separation he was holy, being incessantly employed in religious acts. John Wesley says that grapes were forbidden him for greater caution, to keep him at the farther distance from wine; and that all the days of his separation were sometimes more and sometimes fewer, as he thought fit to appoint.

debates: How long the vow ran: Gill follows the rabbis that a vow expressed absolutely is understood of thirty days, and that the term might run to a thousand days but never fall below thirty; Clarke argues from the ceremony that it was probably never less than a whole year, since the man had to have a full growth of hair to burn under the peace-offering; Wesley leaves the term wholly to the vower's own appointment

Why the prohibition reaches past wine to the kernel and the husk: Calvin makes it a guard against evasion, since men are crafty in inventing subterfuges and would otherwise have kept their luxuries in dried grapes or pressed juice; Wesley calls it greater caution, to keep him at a farther distance; Gill makes it fitness for prayer and the reading of Scripture; Ellicott makes it symbolic of entire consecration and of abstinence from all the delights of the flesh

What the comparison with the priesthood shows: Ellicott makes it a contrast, this law being stricter than the priests', who were forbidden wine only when entering the tabernacle; Calvin makes it an approach, the Nazarites being separated that they might come near the honour of the priesthood; Keil makes it an equivalence of insignia, the free growth of the hair answering to the golden diadem and the anointing oil

Whether the vow points towards monastic life: Ellicott denies it, holding the ideal to be not seclusion but action and uninterrupted devotion; Calvin attacks the monks for boasting angelical perfection while refusing to abstain from wine, their austerity in food purchasing them greater licence in drink
outliers: Calvin's charge that the Carthusians would glory in being martyrs rather than eat meat in a case of necessity, while making their food-austerity a warrant for drinking
Calvin's rule that a sober use of wine is a chief part of temperate living, since those who are not abstemious will sooner take common food than be deprived of wine
Clarke's six-point summary of what the vow consisted in, from the consecration itself down to the incessant employment in religious acts
Ellicott's note that the love of cakes made of raisins is coupled in Hosea with idolatry
Gill's citation of Aben Ezra, that many transgressions are occasioned by wine, which intoxicates the mind, excites lust and unfits for religious duties
The conjecture Clarke reports, that the leper figured man fallen and the Nazarite man in innocence, the vine being forbidden because the tree of knowledge was itself a vine

6.pericope_label: No dead body to be approached, and the offerings when a sudden death defiles the vow

schools.summary: Gill says the phrase, all the days that he separateth himself unto the Lord, is repeated at every new article and branch of the law of the Nazarites, of which what follows is the third, showing that each part of it during that time was strictly to be observed. He shall not make himself unclean for his father or for his mother, Gill says, to which Aben Ezra adds also for his wife and for his daughter and for others; what even the priests of the Lord, the common priests, might do, a Nazarite might not, nor come near any of his relations when dead, as to touch them, to close their eyes or wash their bodies, and provide for their funeral and attend that, or to be where they were. In this respect they were upon a level with the high priest, who was forbidden the same, which shows how sacred these persons were, Gill says; and this may instruct spiritual Nazarites to abstain from the company and conversation of sinners, dead in trespasses and sins, and from all dead works and sinful actions, which, as they are deserving of death, are defiling. All the days of his separation he is holy unto the Lord, Gill continues, set apart for his service, separate from all others, especially the dead, and under obligation to abstain from drinking wine, from shaving his hair and from defiling himself for the dead, and to be employed in holy and religious exercises during the time his vow is upon him. Of the sudden death Gill says it may be in the place where the Nazarite is, whether house or field, a public or private place, or in the tent where he is, as Jarchi says; there are two words we render very suddenly, which many take to be synonymous, two being used to increase the sense, but others think they have a different meaning, the Targums of Onkelos and Jonathan rendering them suddenly through ignorance, understanding it of a chance matter, as when one man is killed by another not wilfully and through malice but without design, while Jarchi interprets the first of them by violence and the latter through error or mistake, so as to include both cases. Of the offering Gill says the two turtles or two young pigeons were not a turtledove and a young pigeon, as Ben Gersom observes, but two of one of the sorts, which was the offering of the poorer sort of childbearing women at their purification and of profluvious persons; and this case of the Nazarite's, being an uncleanness, could not be purged away but by sacrifice, which was typical of the sacrifice of Christ, by which that unclean thing sin is put away for ever, even the sins of holy things being removed in no other way. One of the birds was for a sin offering and one for a burnt offering, both being necessary, the one to expiate sin and the other as a gift to God by way of thankfulness for acceptance of the former; and he was to begin his account again from the time of his shaving his head, and devote as many days to the service of the Lord as he had vowed before. Calvin says that this too they had in common with the high priest, that they were not even to mourn for their relations. Although Moses enjoins two things, that the Nazarites should make themselves unclean neither by entering the house of mourning nor by mourning themselves, it was indeed a duty of humanity to bury the dead, Calvin says; but if any of the people had touched a dead body, or had come near a death-bed or bier, they were polluted, and God demands more of the Nazarites, for it was not sufficient for them to purify themselves according to the accustomed means, but it behoved them to be far removed from all things that would pollute them. Why the touch of a dead body was a pollution Calvin reserves for its proper place, concluding briefly that because by death is represented God's curse, the wages of sin, the Israelites were thus admonished to beware of dead works, as the Apostle calls them. As to the mourning, the reason of the prohibition was different, Calvin says, namely that those who professed the special service of God should set an example to others of magnanimity and submission. If it were sinful to weep and lament when our friends are taken from us, Christ would not have wept at the tomb of Lazarus; but because perturbation is always associated with grief, and men in their mourning are too apt to give way to ambition and pomp, and voluntarily and purposely provoke themselves to excess, as though nature did not already carry them further than is right, the Nazarites could not give an example of moderation if they had mixed themselves with mourners. Wherefore, as they were before restrained from daintiness, so now a remedy is applied to the opposite disease, that is, to sorrow, Calvin says; and although all ought to seek to indulge it moderately, yet something more is prescribed to the Nazarites, that, as if disentangled and stripped from earthly affections, they should go further than the rest of the people. Of the sudden defilement Calvin says that here is prescribed what must be done if a defilement should have been contracted which no precaution could have prevented: if a Nazarite should have willingly and knowingly entered a house of mourning, or should have come near a dead body, his consecration would have been violated not without sin, but in the case of a sudden death the error was excusable, though God commands that it should be expiated, for whatever time of the vow had passed he counts for nothing. This was no light punishment, that he who had been guilty of no fault should begin to pay his vow altogether afresh, Calvin says; besides the loss of the time a sacrifice is also added, whereby he who was polluted should prepare himself for a new consecration. But because this consecration was voluntary, none could complain of the immoderate rigour to which he had subjected himself of his own accord; and meanwhile it was shown how precious to God is the purity of his worship. Of the two Hebrew words Calvin says they are from different roots though of kindred signification, and that it is a rule of Hebrew grammar that the use of two synonymous words is to be considered a mode of expressing a superlative, by which mode of speaking Moses wished more fully to express the unexpected nature of the death; for, in his opinion, it is puerile of the Jews to understand the first of a bloody murder and the other of a sudden death.

Keil and Delitzsch say that because the Nazarite wore the diadem of his God upon his head in the growth of his hair, and was holy to the Lord during the whole period of his consecration, he was to approach no dead person during that time, not even to defile himself for his parents or his brothers and sisters when they died, according to the law laid down for the high priest in Leviticus; consequently, as a matter of course, he was to guard most scrupulously against other defilements, not only like ordinary Israelites but also like the priests, and Samson's mother too was not allowed to eat anything unclean during the period of her pregnancy. If any one died suddenly in a moment by him, that is, in his neighbourhood, and he therefore involuntarily defiled his consecrated head, Keil says, he was to shave his head on the day of his purification, that is, on the seventh day, not because such uncleanness was more especially caught and retained by the hair, as Knobel fancies, but because it was the diadem of his God, the ornament of his condition, which was sanctified to God. On the eighth day, that is to say, on the day after the legal purification, Keil continues, he was then to bring a yearling sheep as a trespass-offering, and the days that were before were to fall, that is, the days of consecration that had already elapsed were not to be reckoned on account of their having fallen, because his consecration had become unclean; he was therefore to commence the whole time of his consecration entirely afresh, and to observe it as required by the vow, and to this end he was to bring a trespass-offering, as a payment or recompense for being reinstated in the former state of consecration. Charles Ellicott says the law of the Nazirite in this respect was equally stringent with that of the high priest and more stringent than that which was imposed upon the priests generally; and that the word rendered the consecration is better rendered the separation, the Hebrew nezer, as also in the ninth verse. The word which is rendered offer, Ellicott says, like the Greek verb, means literally to do, its sacrificial signification in this place being entirely dependent upon the context; and by the dead means by reason of, or on account of, the dead body with which he had been brought in contact.

Adam Clarke says that the consecration of his God is upon his head means literally the separation of his God is upon his head, meaning his hair, which was the proof and emblem of his separation. Now as the hair of the Nazarite was a token of his subjection to God through all the peculiarities of his nazarate, Clarke says, a woman who is married is considered as a Nazarite for life, that is, separated from all others and joined to one husband who is her lord; hence St Paul, probably alluding to this circumstance, says that the woman ought to have power upon her head, that is, wear her hair and veil, for this hair is a proof of her nazarate and of her being in subjection to her husband, as the Nazarite was under subjection to the Lord by the rule of his order. Of the offering Clarke notes that the two turtles or two young pigeons are the same kind of offering made by him who had an issue in Leviticus. John Wesley says that in the matter of his father the Nazarite was equal to the high priest, being in some sort as eminent a type of Christ, and therefore justly required to prefer the service of God, to which he had so fully given himself, before the expressions of his affections to his dearest and nearest relations; and that the consecration means the token of his consecration, namely his long hair. He shall shave his head, Wesley says, because his whole body and especially his hair was defiled by such an accident, which he ought to impute either to his own heedlessness or to God's providence so ordering the matter, possibly for the punishment of his other sins, or for the quickening of him to more purity and detestation of all dead works whereby he would be defiled. A sin offering was required, Wesley says, because such a pollution was, though not his sin, yet the chastisement of his sin; he sinned means that he contracted a ceremonial uncleanness, which is called sinning because it was a type of sin and a violation of a law, though through ignorance and inadvertency; and to hallow means to begin again to hallow or consecrate. The days of his separation means as many days as he had before vowed to God, and lost is in the Hebrew fall, to the ground, that is, be void or of none effect.

debates: What the two words rendered very suddenly mean: Gill transmits the rabbinic division, the Targums giving suddenly through ignorance and Jarchi taking the first of violence and the second of error, so that both cases are covered; Calvin holds the pair to be simply the Hebrew idiom for a superlative, expressing how unexpected the death was, and calls it puerile of the Jews to distinguish a bloody murder from a sudden death

Whether the man who is defiled by a sudden death is at fault: Calvin says he was guilty of no fault, and defends the loss of his elapsed days on the ground that the vow was voluntary and that the purity of God's worship is precious; Wesley tells him to impute the accident either to his own heedlessness or to God's providence, possibly for the punishment of his other sins

Why the defiled head had to be shaved: Keil rejects Knobel's explanation that such uncleanness was especially caught and retained by the hair, and grounds it instead on the hair being the diadem of his God and the ornament of his condition; Wesley says simply that his whole body, and especially his hair, was defiled by the accident

Whether the Nazarite is a type of Christ: Wesley says he was in this equal to the high priest, being in some sort as eminent a type of Christ, where Clarke had denied a few verses earlier that either analogy or proof could be produced for the type
outliers: Calvin's argument that grief is not itself sinful, since Christ would not otherwise have wept at the tomb of Lazarus, the danger lying in the pomp and excess that attend mourning
Calvin's pairing of the two prohibitions as remedies for opposite diseases, daintiness on the one hand and sorrow on the other
Clarke's extension of the nazarate to the married woman, separated from all others and joined to one husband, her hair being the proof of it
Gill's note that the two birds were the offering of the poorer sort of childbearing women and of profluvious persons
Keil's observation that Samson's mother was forbidden anything unclean during her pregnancy
Ellicott's remark that the verb rendered offer means literally to do, its sacrificial force depending wholly on the context

13.pericope_label: The law of the Nazarite at the fulfilling of his days: burnt, sin and peace offerings

schools.summary: Gill says that this is the law of the Nazarite has respect either to what goes before, those being the things he is obliged to who vows the vow of a Nazarite, what he is to abstain from during the time of his vow and what he is to do in case of any defilement, or to what follows after, what is binding upon him, what offerings he is to bring, and what rites and ceremonies are to be observed by him when he has finished his vow. The Nazarite was to present his offering at the door of the tabernacle, to the priest, Gill says, in order to be offered for him to the Lord; and of the basket he notes that unleavened bread was used as at the consecration of Aaron and his sons, though for peace offerings for thanksgiving leavened bread was offered. The priest was to bring them before the Lord, Gill says, that is, all the above offerings to the altar of burnt offering, and there present them to the Lord in the name of the Nazarite. Calvin says Moses now shows at last how, after the full period of the vow, the Nazarites must return to their common life; and first he commands them to place themselves at the door of the tabernacle, then to offer there a lamb without spot for a burnt-offering, a ewe-lamb for a sin-offering, and a ram for peace-offerings, with cakes of fine flour mingled with oil, wafers and unleavened bread, and meat-offering and drink-offerings. As to the peace-offering, Calvin says, because it was presented in thanksgiving it was by no means inappropriate, nor the burnt-offering either, because they might justly congratulate themselves and celebrate God's goodness when they had discharged their pious duty, since God had vouchsafed them no ordinary honour. But what was meant by the sin-offering may be questioned, Calvin says, since expiation was needless for the pure and holy; and here we clearly perceive that however cheerfully and earnestly men endeavour to offer themselves altogether to God, yet they never attain to the goal of perfection, nor arrive at what they desire, but are always exposed to God's judgment unless he should pardon their sins. Whence it appears how base is the Papists' folly, Calvin continues, when they dream of appeasing God by works of supererogation; for if ever any supererogation were pleasing to God, the holiness of the Nazarites, being testified to by the Law, was worthy of this honour, yet God, when the work is complete, commands them to confess their guilt, and suffers not this service to intrude into the place of merit, but requires of them a sacrifice, that they may borrow from elsewhere what belongs not to themselves, though they appear to be the most perfect of all men.

Keil and Delitzsch say the directions as to the release from consecration are called the law of the Nazarite because the idea of the Nazarite's vows culminated in the sacrificial festival which terminated the consecration, and it was in this that it attained to its fullest manifestation. On the day of the completion of the days of his consecration, that is, on the day when the time of consecration expired, Keil says, the Nazarite was to bring to the tabernacle, or offer as his gifts to the Lord, a sheep of a year old as a burnt-offering and an ewe of a year old as a sin-offering, the latter as an expiation for the sins committed involuntarily during the period of consecration, the former as an embodiment of that surrender of himself, body and soul, to the Lord, upon which every act of worship should rest; and in addition to this he was to bring a ram without blemish as a peace-offering, together with a basket of unleavened cakes and wafers baked. The sin-offering and burnt-offering were carried out according to the general instructions, Keil says, and the completion of the consecration vow was concentrated in the preparation of the ram and the basket of unleavened bread for the peace-offering, along with the appropriate meat-offering and drink-offering. Charles Ellicott says the word which is here rendered offer is different from that which is used earlier in the chapter, and means literally to bring near; the cognate noun is Corban, a word which St Mark translates into Greek by a term meaning a gift, and which means a gift offered to God. The sin-offering, Ellicott says, was an offering of atonement for sins committed during the period of the consecration of the Nazirite, and the burnt-offering typified the entire consecration of the body, soul and spirit of the offerer to the Lord; and their meat offering and their drink offerings means the offerings of fine flour and oil and wine which belonged to the burnt-offerings and the peace-offerings.

John Wesley says that by the sin-offering the Nazarite confessed his miscarriages, notwithstanding the strictness of his vow and all the diligence which he could use, and consequently acknowledged his need of the grace of God in Christ Jesus the true Nazarite. The peace-offerings were for thankfulness to God, Wesley says, who had given him grace to make and in some measure to keep such a vow; so he offered all the three sorts of offerings, that he might so far fulfil all righteousness and profess his obligation to observe the will of God in all things. Of the accompanying offering Wesley says only that the meal-offering was such as generally accompanied the sacrifices.

debates: What the sin-offering at the close of a faithfully kept vow is for: Calvin and Wesley make it a confession that no man attains perfection, Calvin turning it against the doctrine of supererogation on the ground that if any work were worthy of that honour the Nazarite's would be, and yet God requires him to confess guilt and borrow from elsewhere what is not his own; Keil and Ellicott give it the narrower use of expiating sins actually committed during the period of consecration, Keil specifying the involuntary ones

What the phrase this is the law of the Nazarite governs: Gill allows it to look either backward to the obligations and the rules for defilement, or forward to the offerings and rites of release; Keil argues for the forward reference and grounds it on the idea of the vow culminating in the sacrificial festival that terminated it

Whether Christ is the Nazarite the law figures: Wesley calls him the true Nazarite in explaining the sin-offering, continuing the typology that Clarke had refused earlier in the chapter and that Calvin and Henry had affirmed in their own terms

What the unleavened bread signifies here: Gill notes that peace offerings of thanksgiving normally required leavened bread, so that this basket follows the pattern of the consecration of Aaron and his sons instead; Keil takes the ram and the basket together as the point in which the completion of the vow was concentrated
outliers: Calvin's argument that the Nazarite's holiness, if any work could be, was the likeliest candidate for merit, and that God nevertheless required a sacrifice of him
Ellicott's derivation of the verb rendered offer from a root meaning to bring near, whose cognate noun is Corban
Gill's note that leavened bread belonged to peace offerings of thanksgiving, but unleavened bread to this occasion and to the consecration of Aaron
Keil's description of the burnt-offering as the embodiment of a surrender of body and soul on which every act of worship should rest
Wesley's qualification that God gave the man grace to make, and in some measure to keep, such a vow

18.pericope_label: The shaving of the head, the hair burned under the peace-offering, and the wave offering

schools.summary: Gill says the Targum of Jonathan renders the direction that the Nazarite shall shave the head of his separation without, that is, without the tabernacle, at the door of it where the people assembled together, so that this was to be done publicly, that it might be known of all, and no offence taken at the Nazarite's drinking wine and concerning himself for the dead and attending funerals, for by this action it was known that his Nazariteship was at an end. Whereas the hair of the Nazarite was consecrated to the Lord by his vow, Gill says, and this vow being punctually fulfilled it was sacred, and to be presented to the Lord, and to be of no use and service to himself or others, and therefore to be all clean shaven off; for, as Maimonides says, if two hairs only were left, nothing was done, and the command of shaving was not kept. Of the shoulder Gill says it was the left shoulder, for the right shoulder, which is the heave shoulder of every peace offering, belonged to the priest by another law; and by this law of the Nazarite he had also the other shoulder, and so had both, which was peculiar to this case, the vow of the Nazarite being a very sacred thing and he being enabled to perform it, so that a greater expression of gratitude for it was expected and required of him; and this shoulder was taken out of the pot in which it was boiled. The priest was to wave them for a wave offering before the Lord, Gill says, putting his hands under the Nazarite's, as in other cases where this ceremony was used, and so moving them to and fro, backwards and forwards, upwards and downwards, testifying hereby the goodness of God unto him, his sovereign dominion over him, that all he had depended on him and was received from him, and that all he did, particularly in keeping his vow of Nazariteship, was through his assistance, and for which he made this grateful acknowledgment by delivering the above to the priest. This is the law of the Nazarite who hath vowed, Gill adds, that is, what he is obliged to do when his Nazariteship is up.

Keil and Delitzsch say the Nazarite had also to shave his consecrated head and put the hair into the altar-fire under the peace-offering that was burning, and thus hand over and sacrifice to the Lord the hair of his head which had been worn in honour of him. When this had been done, Keil says, the priest took the boiled shoulder of the ram, with an unleavened cake and wafer out of the basket, and placed these pieces in the hands of the Nazarite, and waved them before Jehovah; they then became the portion of the priest, in addition to the wave-breast and heave-leg which fell to the priest in the case of every peace-offering, to set forth the participation of the Lord in the sacrificial meal. But the fact that, in addition to these, the boiled shoulder was given up symbolically to the Lord through the process of waving, together with a cake and wafer, was intended to indicate that the table-fellowship with the Lord, shadowed forth in the sacrificial meal of the peace-offering, took place here in a higher degree, Keil says, inasmuch as the Lord directed a portion of the Nazarite's meal to be handed over to his representatives and servants. After that the Nazarite might drink wine again, Keil adds, probably at the sacrificial meal, after the Lord had received his share of the sacrifice and the release from consecration had thus been completed. Of the closing verse he says the meaning is, this is the law of the Nazarite who vowed his sacrificial gifts to the Lord on the ground of his consecration, that is, who offered his sacrifice in accordance with the state of a Nazarite into which he had entered; for the sacrifices mentioned earlier were not the object of a special vow, but contained in the vow of the Nazarite and therefore already vowed, as Knobel observes. Beside what his hand grasps means what he is otherwise able to perform, Keil says, so that according to the measure of his vow he had to offer the sacrifices previously mentioned on the ground of his consecration vow, and beyond that he was free to vow anything else according to his ability, and to present other sacrificial gifts to the Lord for his sanctuary and his servants. Charles Ellicott says the consignment of his hair to the sacrificial fire formed a solemn and suitable termination of the days of his separation to the Lord during the continuance of his Nazirite vow; and that beside that that his hand shall get means besides any voluntary offerings which it may be in his power to make.

Adam Clarke says the hair was permitted to grow for this purpose, and that as the Nazarite was a kind of sacrifice offered to God through the whole term of his nazarate or separation, and no human flesh or blood could be offered on the altar of the Lord, he offered his hair at the conclusion of his separation as a sacrifice, that hair which was the token of his complete subjection to the Lord and which was now considered as the Lord's property. The Hindoos, after a vow, do not cut their hair during the term of their vow, Clarke notes, but at the expiration of it they shave it off at the place where the vow was made; and that the hair of the head was superstitiously used among different nations he has had occasion to remark elsewhere. That the Gentiles might have learned this from the Jews is possible, Clarke says, though some learned men think that this consecration of the hair to a deity was in use among the heathens before the time of Moses, and in nations who had no intercourse or connection with the Jews. Of the closing verse Clarke reports from Maimonides, in his Treatise of the Nazarite, that a man might become a Nazarite in behalf of another, that is, might assist him in bearing the expenses of the sacrifices: a son may fulfil the vow his deceased father hath made but did not live to accomplish; he that saith, upon me be the shaving of a Nazarite, is bound to bring the offerings of shaving for cleanness, and may offer them by the hand of what Nazarite he will; and if he say, upon me be half the oblations of a Nazarite, then he bringeth half the offerings by what Nazarite he will, and that Nazarite payeth his offerings out of that which is his. By this, Clarke quotes Ainsworth as saying, we may see the reason of that which James said to Paul, though he had no Nazarite's vow upon him, that there were four men who had a vow on them, whom Paul should take and sanctify himself with them and be at charges with them, that they might shave their heads; for though Paul had not vowed or fulfilled a Nazariteship himself, yet he might contribute with them and partake of their charges about the sacrifices. John Wesley says the shaving was to be at the door publicly, that it might be known that his vow was ended and therefore that he was at liberty as to those things from which he had restrained himself for a season, since otherwise some might have been scandalised at his use of his liberty; and the fire is that upon which the flesh of the peace-offerings was boiled. The shoulder, Wesley says, is the left shoulder, as appears from the next verse where this is joined with the heave shoulder, which was the right shoulder and which was the priest's due in all sacrifices and in this also; but here the other shoulder was added to it, as a special token of thankfulness from the Nazarites for God's singular favours vouchsafed unto them. Into the hands means that the Nazarite may give them to the priest as his peculiar gift; and beside that that his hand shall get means besides what he shall voluntarily give according to his ability.

debates: Why the priest received both shoulders here and only one elsewhere: Gill and Wesley agree that the addition was a token of gratitude required of a man who had been enabled to perform so sacred a vow; Keil grounds it instead on the symbolism of the waving, that the table-fellowship with the Lord shadowed forth in every peace-offering took place here in a higher degree

Why the hair had to be burned: Clarke argues that the Nazarite was himself a kind of sacrifice, and that since no human flesh or blood could be offered on the altar he offered his hair in its stead; Keil says simply that he handed over to the Lord the hair worn in his honour; Gill takes it from the hair's being consecrated and so of no use to himself or others

Whether the practice of consecrating hair was borrowed: Clarke allows that the Gentiles might have learned it from the Jews, but reports the opinion of some that it was in use before Moses and in nations having no connection with them, which agrees with Keil's earlier refusal to derive the Nazarite vow from Egypt

What beside that that his hand shall get covers: Ellicott and Wesley take it of voluntary offerings within the man's ability; Keil adds, on Knobel's authority, that the sacrifices already named were not separately vowed but contained in the Nazarite vow itself, so that only what lies beyond them is free
outliers: Clarke's report from Maimonides that a man might be a Nazarite on another's behalf by bearing part of the charges, and that a son might fulfil a vow his father did not live to accomplish
Ainsworth's application of that practice, quoted by Clarke, to explain how Paul could be at charges with four men who had a vow though he had none himself
Clarke's comparison with the Hindoos, who let the hair grow through a vow and shave it at the place where the vow was made
Gill's citation of Maimonides that if two hairs only were left, nothing was done and the command of shaving was not kept
Gill's description of the waving, the priest's hands under the Nazarite's, moving to and fro, backwards and forwards, upwards and downwards
Keil's note that the Nazarite drank wine again probably at the sacrificial meal, once the Lord had received his share

22.pericope_label: The Aaronic blessing: the Lord bless thee and keep thee, and they shall put my name upon Israel

schools.summary: Gill says the Lord spake unto Moses at the same time perhaps that the law was given concerning the Nazarites, though why this should follow upon that, and what connection there is between the one and the other, it is not easy to say; the Nazarites were holy persons and so were the priests, and therefore, according to Aben Ezra and others, the law of the one is joined to the law of the other. Aaron and his sons that succeeded him in all after generations, being the persons who were in a public manner to bless the people of Israel, are particularly addressed. Of the blessing itself Gill says the word Jehovah is three times used, and a different accent put to each word, denoting three distinct persons and one Jehovah, who are each of them concerned in the blessing of the Lord's people, the spiritual Israel of God: Jehovah the Father blesses with all spiritual blessings, with electing, adopting, justifying and pardoning grace, with regenerating and calling and persevering grace, and with eternal life; Jehovah the Son blesses particularly with redeeming grace and has a concern in all the other blessings, the saints being blessed with them in him; and Jehovah the Spirit blesses as a spirit of regeneration and sanctification, as the spirit of faith, as a comforter, as the spirit of adoption, and as the earnest and sealer of the saints unto the day of redemption. The Lord make his face to shine upon thee means, Gill says, cause himself, the sun of righteousness, to arise and shine upon them, and give both spiritual light and heat unto them, granting his gracious presence, the manifestations of himself, communion with him, and clearer discoveries of his love; and the Lord lift up his countenance upon thee means show his face and favour, look cheerfully on his people, declare himself well pleased with them in Christ, and appear as smiling upon them through him, indulging them with visits of love and restoring to them the joys of his salvation. They shall put my name upon the children of Israel, Gill says, that is, call them by his name, the people of the Lord, call upon the name of the Lord to bless them, and pronounce the blessing on them in the name of the Lord, in or by the name Jehovah, as Jarchi says, three times used in this form of blessing. And I will bless them means really and truly bless them, with all sorts of blessings temporal and spiritual, with solid and substantial ones, such as are irrevocable and irreversible; and unless the Lord blesses, Gill says, in vain do the priests bless, or any of his ministers pronounce a blessing, for theirs lies in words and wishes, his in real facts; they can only pray and wish for the blessing, it is he only that can give it, and confirm what they pronounce. Some refer the relative them to the priests, Gill notes, as if the sense were that God will bless the priests that bless Israel, for God will bless them that bless his people, but Aben Ezra thinks it belongs to both. Calvin says a part of the sacerdotal duties, of which mention is constantly made in the Law, is here briefly set forth, for God says that he had appointed the priests to bless the people, to which David seems to allude when he says, we have blessed you out of the house of the Lord. This doctrine is especially profitable, Calvin says, that believers may confidently assure themselves that God is reconciled to them, when he ordains the priests to be witnesses and heralds of his paternal favour towards them. The word to bless is often used for to pray for blessings, which is the common duty of all pious persons, but this rite was an efficacious testimony of God's grace, as if the priests bore from his own mouth the commandment to bless; and Luke shows that this was truly fulfilled in Christ, when he relates that he lifted up his hands, according to the solemn rite of the Law, to bless his disciples. In these words the priests were appointed ambassadors to reconcile God to the people, Calvin says, and this in the person of Christ, who is the only sufficient surety of God's grace and blessing; inasmuch, therefore, as they then were types of Christ, they were commanded to bless the people. But it is worthy of remark, he adds, that they are commanded to pronounce the form of benediction audibly, and not to offer prayers in an obscure whisper, and hence we gather that they preached God's grace, which the people might apprehend by faith. Blessing is an act of God's genuine liberality, Calvin says, because the abundance of all good things is derived to us from his favour as their only source; and by the clause that he should keep the people he intimates that he is the sole defender of the Church and protects it under his guardianship. But since the main advantage of God's grace consists in our sense of it, the words make his face shine on you are added, for nothing is more desirable for the consummation of our happiness than that we should behold the serene countenance of God; and Calvin interprets the clause so, that the people may perceive and taste the sweetness of God's goodness, which may cheer them like the brightness of the sun when it illumines the world in serene weather. Immediately afterwards the people are recalled to the first cause, God's gratuitous mercy, which alone reconciles him to us when we should otherwise by our own deserts be hated by him. That the Lord lift up his countenance upon thee is a common phrase of Scripture, Calvin says, meaning, may God remember his people, not that forgetfulness can occur in him, but because we suppose that he has cast away his care of us unless he actually gives proof of his anxiety for our welfare. Finally it is added that he may establish peace upon his people, which others translate a little less literally, put thee into peace; and since this word signifies not only rest and a tranquil state but also all prosperity and success, Calvin willingly embraces this latter sense, although even its proper signification is not disagreeable to him. His editor quotes Ainsworth, that peace generally signifies all prosperity and the perfect enjoying of all good things, being opposed to war, to discord and enmity, to tumult and confusion, and to all adversity, and that it is therefore added for a conclusion of blessings, this peace being obtained by Jesus Christ and enjoyed by the Holy Ghost. Of the last verse Calvin says that although others have rightly translated it, they shall call upon my name, yet since the Hebrew phrase is emphatic he has preferred retaining it, for God deposits his name with the priests, that they may daily bring it forward as a pledge of his good will and of the salvation which proceeds from thence. The promise finally subjoined gives assurance that this was no empty or useless ceremony, Calvin says, when God declares that he will bless the people; and hence we gather that whatsoever the ministers of the Church do by God's command is ratified by him with a real and solid result, since he declares nothing by his ministers which he will not himself fulfil and perform by the efficacy of his Spirit. But we must observe, Calvin adds, that he does not so transfer the office of blessing to his priests as to resign this right to them, for after having entrusted this ministry to them he claims the accomplishment of the thing for himself alone.

Matthew Henry says the priests, among other good offices which they were to do, are appointed solemnly to bless the people in the name of the Lord, and that it was part of their work; hereby God put an honour upon the priests, for the less is blessed of the better, and hereby he gave great comfort and satisfaction to the people, who looked upon the priest as God's mouth to them. Though the priest of himself could do no more than beg a blessing, Henry says, yet being an intercessor by office, and doing that in his name who commands the blessing, the prayer carried with it a promise, and he pronounced it as one having authority, with his hands lifted up and his face towards the people. This was a type of Christ's errand into the world, which was to bless us, as the high priest of our profession, Henry says, for the last thing he did on earth was with uplifted hands to bless his disciples; and he observes as a tradition of the Jews, reported by the learned bishop Pearson, that the priests blessed the people only at the close of the morning sacrifice and not of the evening sacrifice, to show that in the last days, the days of the Messiah, which are as it were the evening of the world, the benediction of the law should cease and the blessing of Christ should take place. It was also a pattern to gospel ministers, Henry says, the masters of assemblies, who are in like manner to dismiss their solemn assemblies with a blessing, since the same that are God's mouth to his people to teach and command them are his mouth likewise to bless them, and those that receive the law shall receive the blessing. The Hebrew doctors warn the people, he adds, that they say not, what availeth the blessing of this poor simple priest, for, say they, the receiving of the blessing depends not on the priest but on the holy blessed God. In their other devotions no form was prescribed, Henry says, but this being God's command concerning benediction, that it might not look like anything of their own, he puts the very words in their mouths. The blessing is commanded upon each particular person, Henry observes: they must each of them prepare themselves to receive the blessing, and then they should find enough in it to make every man happy; if we take the law to ourselves, we may take the blessing to ourselves, as if our names were inserted. The name Jehovah is three times repeated in it, and, as the critics observe, each with a different accent in the original, so that the Jews themselves think there is some mystery in this, and we know what it is, Henry says, the New Testament having explained it, which directs us to expect the blessing from the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of the Father, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, each of which persons is Jehovah, and yet they are not three Lords but one Lord. The favour of God is all in all in this blessing, Henry says, for that is the fountain of all good: our blessing God is only our speaking well of him, his blessing us is doing well for us, and those whom he blesses are blessed indeed. The Lord make his face shine upon thee alludes to the shining of the sun upon the earth, to enlighten and comfort it and to renew the face of it, meaning, the Lord love thee and cause thee to know that he loves thee, for we cannot but be happy if we have God's love and cannot but be easy if we know that we have it; and the Lord lift up his countenance upon thee seems to allude to the smiles of a father upon his child, or of a man upon his friend whom he takes pleasure in, so that if God give us the assurances of his special favour this will put gladness into the heart. The fruits of this favour, Henry says, are protection from evil, for it is he that keeps Israel and neither slumbers nor sleeps, pardon of sin, and peace.

Keil and Delitzsch say the spiritual character of the congregation of Israel culminated in the blessing with which the priests were to bless the people, and that the directions as to this blessing impressed the seal of perfection upon the whole order and organisation of the people of God, inasmuch as Israel was first truly formed into a congregation of Jehovah by the fact that God not only bestowed his blessing upon it, but placed the communication of this blessing in the hands of the priests, the chosen and constant mediators of the blessings of his grace, and imposed it upon them as one portion of their official duty. The blessing which the priests were to impart consisted of a triple blessing of two members each, Keil says, which stood related to each other thus, that the second in each case contained a special application of the first to the people, and the three gradations unfolded the substance of the blessing step by step with ever increasing emphasis, the first conveying the blessing in the most general form. This blessing was not to remain merely a pious wish, however, Keil says, but to be manifested in the people with all the power of a blessing from God, and this assurance closes the divine command, that they shall put God's name upon the children of Israel and he will bless them. Charles Ellicott says the occasions on which this blessing was used are not recorded, and that the blessing itself, which marks in a special manner the spiritual character of the chosen people, consists of three double clauses; in each of these three clauses the sacred name Jehovah is repeated, and there is a rising gradation in the blessing invoked, until it culminates in that peace which is the highest of those gifts that God can bestow and that man can possess. There has been commonly recognised in this blessing an allusion to the doctrine of the Trinity, Ellicott records; and he notes that mention is made in Leviticus of a blessing pronounced by Aaron upon the people, but that no form of words is found there.

Adam Clarke says the prayer which God makes for his followers, and puts into their mouth, we are sure must be right, and to it, when sincerely, faithfully and fervently offered, we may confidently expect an answer; if he condescended to give us a form of blessing or a form of prayer, we may rest assured that he will accept what he himself has made. This consideration may produce great confidence in them who come with either prayer or praise to the throne of grace, Clarke says, both of which should be, as far as circumstances will admit, in the very words of Scripture, for we can readily attach a consequence to the words of God which we shall find difficult to attach to the best ordered words of men. There are three forms of blessing here, Clarke says, any or all of which the priests might use on any occasion, and he gives a verbal translation of each, and then a paraphrase: may God speak good unto thee by giving thee his excellent promises, and preserve thee in the possession of all the good thou hast and from all the evil with which thou art threatened; may the Holy Trinity illuminate thy heart, giving thee the true knowledge of thyself and of thy Maker, and may he show thee his graciousness in pardoning thy sins and supporting thy soul; may God give thee communion with the Father, Son and Spirit, with a constant sense of his approbation, and grant thee prosperity in thy soul and in all thy secular affairs. Several wise and learned men believe that the mystery of the Holy Trinity is not obscurely hinted at in it, Clarke says: God the Father blesses and keeps his followers, God the Son is gracious unto sinners in remitting their offences which he died to blot out, and God the Holy Spirit takes of the things which are Christ's and shows them unto genuine Christians, and diffuses the peace of God in their hearts; in a word, Christ, the gift of the Father by the energy of the Holy Spirit, came to bless every one of us by turning us away from our iniquities. Clarke closes the chapter by saying that every genuine Christian is a true Nazarite, separated from the world and dedicated solely to the service of God, that his life is a life of self-denial, that all this enters into the spirit of his baptismal vow, and that the person who is faithful has the blessing of God entailed upon him. John Wesley says the words mean thus, or in these words, yet they were not tied to these very words, because after this we have examples of Moses and David and Solomon blessing the people in other words. Bless thee means bestow upon you all manner of blessings, temporal and spiritual, Wesley says, and keep thee means continue his blessings to thee and preserve thee in and to the use of them, keeping thee from sin and its bitter effects. Shine upon thee alludes to the shining of the sun upon the earth, to enlighten and warm and renew the face of it, meaning, the Lord love thee and make thee know that he loves thee, for we cannot but be happy if we have God's love and cannot but be easy if we know that we have it; lift up his countenance means look upon thee with a cheerful and pleasant countenance, as one that is well pleased with thee and thy services; and peace means peace with God, with thy own conscience and with all men, all prosperity being comprehended under this word. Put my name, Wesley says, means shall call them by my name, shall recommend them to me as my own people, and bless them and pray unto me for them as such, which is a powerful argument to prevail with God for them.

debates: Whether the priestly blessing is prayer or an efficacious act: Calvin distinguishes the common duty of praying for blessings from this rite, which was an efficacious testimony of God's grace, and Keil says it was not to remain a pious wish but to be manifested with all the power of a blessing from God; Henry holds both, that of himself the priest could only beg but by office his prayer carried a promise; Gill is the most deflationary, that the priests' part lies in words and wishes and God's in real facts

Whether the prescribed words bind: Wesley says they were not tied to these very words, since Moses and David and Solomon afterwards blessed in others; Henry says God put the very words in their mouths precisely that the blessing might not look like anything of their own; Clarke goes further and urges that prayer and praise alike should be, so far as circumstances allow, in the very words of Scripture

What the threefold form signifies: Henry, Gill and Clarke find the Trinity in the three repetitions of the name, Henry adding that the accents differ and that the New Testament has explained the mystery; Ellicott records that reading as commonly recognised but offers instead a rising gradation culminating in peace, and Keil describes the architecture alone, each second member applying the first with increasing emphasis

How far the blessing is transferred to the priests: Calvin insists that God does not resign the right in entrusting the ministry, but claims the accomplishment for himself alone; Gill reports a reading of the closing promise that refers the blessing to the priests themselves, which Aben Ezra extends to both

Why the blessing follows the law of the Nazarite: Gill admits it is not easy to say what the connection is, and offers only Aben Ezra's suggestion that both concern holy persons; Keil sees the whole order of the people sealed by it, Israel being first truly formed into a congregation of Jehovah when God placed the communication of his blessing in priestly hands
outliers: Bishop Pearson's tradition, reported by Henry, that the priests blessed only after the morning sacrifice and not the evening, to show that in the evening of the world the benediction of the law should give place to the blessing of Christ
Calvin's insistence that the form be pronounced audibly and not in an obscure whisper, from which he gathers that the priests preached God's grace
Ainsworth's note, quoted by Calvin's editor, that peace is opposed to war, to discord, to tumult and to all adversity, and is therefore set as the conclusion of blessings
Ellicott's observation that the occasions on which the blessing was used are nowhere recorded
Henry's remark that the blessing is commanded upon each particular person, so that we may take it to ourselves as if our names were inserted
Clarke's closing application that every genuine Christian is a true Nazarite, separated from the world and dedicated solely to the service of God
